story:
Colton had signed up for the Environmental Justice club thinking he'd learn about recycling, but instead Mr. Huang had assigned him to research the Amazon rainforest's nutrient cycles for the spring presentation. He spent three days reading articles that mostly contradicted each other. One scientist claimed the soil was so depleted that the rainforest shouldn't exist at all. Another said phosphorus mysteriously arrived there every year. The mystery frustrated him more than the assignment itself.

"Why don't you just ask someone?" his friend Marcus suggested at lunch, but Colton wanted to figure it out first. He didn't want to seem like he hadn't done the work. That evening, he sat in the library with his laptop, scrolling through research papers until one title caught his attention: "Intercontinental Dust Transport and Rainforest Ecology." The author, Dr. Elena Rojas, described how winds carry millions of tons of dust from the Sahara across the Atlantic every year, and that dust contains phosphorus that fertilizes the Amazon rainforest, whose own soils are poor in that nutrient.

Colton read it twice. The Sahara was in Africa. The Amazon was in South America. That was an entire ocean between them. He wanted to suppress his doubt, to just accept it, but the connection seemed too strange to be real. He decided to test it. If the dust was really that important, then without it, the rainforest should struggle. He created a simple model on his computer, removing the Saharan phosphorus from his calculations of the forest's nutrient balance. The numbers collapsed. The forest couldn't sustain itself with just its own soil. But with the dust included, everything stabilized.

The following Monday, Colton presented his findings to the club. He explained the dust transport and showed his model, waiting for Mr. Huang or someone to correct him. Instead, Mr. Huang nodded and asked, "So what does this tell you about these systems?" The question hung in the air while Colton thought through it properly for the first time. The rainforest wasn't an isolated sanctuary of nature. It depended on a desert thousands of miles away. Neither place could be understood alone.

"It means they're connected," Colton said slowly. "Even if they're far apart, what happens in one place affects the other." Marcus was writing notes, actually paying attention instead of scrolling through his phone. Two other club members leaned forward. Colton found himself wanting to keep explaining, to make them see the lavish complexity of it, the way the whole planet functioned as one system.

After the meeting, Mr. Huang pulled him aside. "That was solid thinking, trying to see what would happen if the phosphorus wasn't there. That's how scientists actually work. They don't just read an answer. They test it." Colton felt something settle in him, a kind of satisfaction that had nothing to do with getting it right on the first try. He'd been wrong about the possibility, and then he'd worked through it.

"Can I keep researching this?" Colton asked. "There's probably more to it." Mr. Huang smiled. "I was hoping you'd say that. Start with Dr. Rojas's other papers." Walking to his next class, Colton pulled up her name on his phone, thinking about dust storms crossing an ocean, about forests blooming thousands of miles away from the source of their strength.

Alexis loved soccer. Every day he played in the schoolyard. But the ball kept flying over his head. The big kids headed it, and he could not.

"I want to be taller," Alexis said. He heard that kids grow at night. So he tried to stay up all night. He squeezed his toy cat until it purred, and he watched the dark tree branch outside his window. But his eyes closed anyway. Sleep pulled him down like a soft blanket.

The next day, Alexis felt slow. The grass was icy, and his feet slipped. He missed the ball again and again. His coach sat with him on the bench. "You look tired," she said. "Try something new tonight."

So Alexis made a plan. First, he put away his ball early. Next, he took a warm bath. Then he read one book in bed. Last, he turned off the light himself. He did it again the next night, and the next. Sleep came fast, and it stayed all night long, nine hours, ten hours, sometimes more.

Day after day, Alexis played in the schoolyard. Then one morning something felt different. The ball flew high, and he jumped. Up went his head, and bump! The ball flew into the goal.

"How did you do that?" asked the big kid.

Alexis looked at the branch above the goal. He remembered standing under it in fall. Now his head was closer to it. He had grown.

"I slept," Alexis said. "First bath, then book, then lights out." The big kid laughed, and Alexis kicked the ball again.

The screen door banged twice before Alicia got it to close properly, and by then her grandfather had already claimed the good chair in front of the television, a glass of iced tea sweating on the side table beside him. It was the third Saturday in a row that she had come over to watch the matches with him, mostly because her parents thought she should know her grandfather better than she did, and partly because there was nothing else to do in a town that shut down when the mill laid off its second shift. Her cousin Deshawn had arrived an hour ago with his chemistry textbook under his arm, which was typical, because Deshawn crammed for everything the night before and then slept through the game.

"Six weeks," Deshawn was saying now, wedged into the corner of the couch. "I studied six whole weeks for that exam. Every Sunday, all afternoon." He pulled the textbook out and dropped it on the cushion between them like evidence in a trial.

Alicia frowned at the screen, where two rowers were fighting through the last five hundred meters of a race, their strokes ragged and desperate. "Weren't you also up until two in the morning on Friday?" she asked. "I could hear you through the wall. You sounded like a dying animal."

"That doesn't count as studying less," Deshawn said. "That's studying harder."

Their grandfather snorted without taking his eyes off the race. On the screen, the British boat edged ahead by half a length, and Alicia noticed something she had been noticing all summer: the crews that sprinted wildly in the middle of the race always seemed to fade at the end, while the ones who held a steady, almost boring rhythm had something left for the final stretch. She wondered whether the rowers could feel the difference, or whether it only looked that way from the shore.

She reached over and flipped Deshawn's textbook open to the front, where he had penciled a calendar of his six weeks. Sunday afternoons, each one circled, and then the last two pages of Friday-night panic scrawled in the margins. "How many hours total?" she asked.

He shrugged. "Like forty, maybe."

"And Tasha took the same class." Tasha was their other cousin, the plodder of the family, the one their aunts described with a small pitying smile because she studied a little every single evening and never once stayed up late. She had gotten the top mark in the class. Deshawn had gotten a seventy-two.

"It's talent," Deshawn said flatly. "She's just smart."

Alicia sat with that for a moment, turning it over the way she turned over the rowing thing. Two explanations, and only one of them could she actually test. Tasha was smart: unfalsifiable, comfortable, explaining nothing. Or the same forty hours spread thin across every day simply stuck better than the same forty hours hammered in on Sundays, with the Sunday knowledge apparently leaking out somewhere between weekends. Was that possible? She tried it against her own life, her own French vocabulary, the words she had crammed for last spring's quiz and could no longer touch, versus the ones she had idly practiced on the bus all year, which still surfaced when she needed them. The evidence seemed to lean one way, though she had to admit the evidence couldn't prove anything. Maybe Tasha was smart. Maybe Deshawn was not. The hours were equal, and the results were not, and that was as far as the counting went.

On the screen the race ended, the winning crew slumping over their oars while the losers sat frozen, and their grandfather raised his glass toward the television as if toasting them all. "The sprinters never learn," he said. "Pace wins regattas."

"Pace wins chemistry," Alicia said, mostly to herself, and Deshawn gave her a suspicious look.

She picked up his textbook before he could object and tore out the penciled calendar page, folding it into her back pocket as a memento of the moment she had half understood something. If she was right, it would be vindicated in June, when she spread her own exam study across every ordinary evening and left the panic to Deshawn. If she was wrong, she would only have lost the thrill of the last-minute scramble, which, watching the exhausted rowers drift past the finish line, she suspected was overrated anyway.

Their grandfather turned the volume up for the next race. Alicia settled deeper into the couch, and Deshawn, after a minute, reached over and took his textbook back.

"Every day, then," he muttered. "A little. Like Tasha."

"Like Tasha," Alicia agreed, and the starting gun cracked through the speakers.

Zachary walked into music class excited because today was the day they would start learning drums. Mrs. Chen had promised something special, and when he saw the shiny silver drums waiting on the stage, he could hardly sit still.

"Today we're learning to read drum notation," Mrs. Chen announced. "It's different from the melody notes you already know." She showed the class a piece of paper covered with symbols on five lines, but these symbols were different from the ones in songbooks. Some symbols sat high on the lines, some sat low, and some floated in between. Zachary stared at the paper. How could he tell which drum to hit? A snare drum hit high sounded totally different from a bass drum hit low, but how did these tiny dots and squiggles tell him which was which?

Mrs. Chen handed out small cardboard boxes and asked the class to poke a tiny hole in one side of each box. "Trust me," she said with a smile. Zachary thought this was strange, but he did it anyway. When Mrs. Chen turned off the lights and had everyone point their boxes toward the bright window, something amazing happened. The upside-down picture of the trees outside appeared on the inside wall of his box, sharp and clear. Zachary gasped. "The light goes straight through the hole," he whispered to himself.

That's when it clicked. The drum notation worked like his box. The position on the lines, the height on the page, it was just like the position of the picture inside the box. High things went high, low things went low, and his eyes could read it in a straight line. He looked back at his drum chart with new understanding. The symbols weren't confusing anymore. They were a map, and he was ready to follow it.

Thomas sat in the band practice room with his saxophone across his lap, listening to the section leader explain the new piece they'd be learning. His stomach felt tight. Ever since he'd gotten braces last month, he'd been self-conscious about how he looked, and he wasn't sure he was doing the right things to keep everything clean. He rinsed his braces after lunch, but sometimes he still felt awkward eating in front of people, worried that food was stuck between the wires.

"Okay, let's try the opening," Mrs. Chen said, lifting her clarinet. The saxophones came in strong, and Thomas played his part, feeling the vibration in his chest. Halfway through, his diaphragm suddenly spasmed and a hiccup burst out of him, loud and unexpected. His face burned red. A few kids giggled. Mrs. Chen smiled gently. "Keep going, everyone," she said, and they restarted.

Over the next week, the hiccups kept happening during practice, always at random moments. Thomas started paying attention to when they came. He noticed they seemed worse on days when he'd been eating quickly at lunch or drinking soda right before rehearsal. One afternoon, he was talking to his friend Marcus between pieces, explaining his theory. "Maybe if I breathe differently, I can stop them," Thomas said. "Like, maybe it's about how my stomach and lungs cooperate?" Marcus shrugged. "My dad says if you hold your breath, it helps."

Thomas decided to test it. The next time they played a passage with long notes, he took a deep breath before starting and held it steady as he played, controlling his breathing completely. When the section finished, he waited. No hiccup. He tried it the next day during a different piece, this time breathing normally but slowly and deliberately, keeping his breaths deep. Again, nothing happened. By the third practice, Thomas realized that when he stayed calm and breathed in a controlled way, the sudden spasms that had been making him embarrassed all week just stopped coming. It wasn't about his braces or his appearance at all; it was something he could actually control.

On Friday, as they worked through the difficult middle section, Thomas played with a confidence he hadn't felt before. When Mrs. Chen finally set down her clarinet and said, "Much better, Thomas, that's a credible performance," he felt something shift inside him. He wasn't worried about being watched anymore. He knew now that some things just needed understanding, a little patience, and the right approach.

Dylan went to art class at the community center. The teacher said, "Today we paint a flag on a tall pole." Dylan wanted to make his flag look real. He painted a sparkly red flag at the top of his pole. But the flag looked stuck. It did not look like it could move.

Then Dylan looked out the window. A man stood on the ground by a real flagpole. A rope went over a wheel at the top. The man pulled down on one end of the rope. The flag went up to the top of the pole! Dylan watched again. Pull down, and up it went. "That wheel is called a pulley," said the teacher. Dylan did not say anything. He just kept watching.

First, Dylan painted a little wheel at the top of his pole. Next, he painted a rope over the wheel. Then, he painted a man on the ground. Last, the man pulled down on his end of the rope. The other end went up, and the flag went up too. His painting looked just like the real thing!

The class went down to the basement for juice. Dylan felt calm and proud. A girl named Mia looked at his painting. "How did you know that?" she asked. Dylan pointed out the window at the flagpole and said, "I watched the real one."

Eva walked into Room 14 and looked for an empty desk. She did not know anyone in this class, and her stomach felt tight. The teacher, Mrs. Chen, smiled and pointed to a seat near the window. "Welcome, Eva. We are starting geometry today," she said, which made Eva feel a little better because she liked shapes.

Mrs. Chen held up a large paper kite. "This kite was beautiful once," she said, "but one corner got bent. Can we fix it?" She showed the class that the kite was made of four triangles joined together. One triangle had two corners that measured 45 degrees and 90 degrees. "We know the kite should fly straight," Mrs. Chen said, "so every triangle must have its three angles add up to exactly 180 degrees. If we know two angles, we can find the third. Who wants to try?"

Eva raised her hand without thinking about it. Mrs. Chen handed her a pencil and paper. Eva thought hard. The broken triangle had one angle of 45 degrees and another of 90 degrees. She added them: 45 plus 90 made 135 degrees. To get to 180 degrees, she needed 45 more degrees. She wrote it down and showed Mrs. Chen. "Yes," Mrs. Chen said, "that is exactly right. Your effort on your first day shows real thinking."

Another student named Marcus asked if they could test it on the actual kite. Mrs. Chen gave each child a protractor, a tool that measures angles. Eva measured the broken corner and saw it was exactly 45 degrees. She turned to another girl named Tasha. "We figured out the answer before measuring it," Eva said. "The math told us what the corner should be."

Tasha's eyes got wide. "That is brilliant," she said. "You can know something before you even look at it." The class included six other students who wanted to measure different triangles now. Mrs. Chen handed out more protractors and shapes. Eva showed Tasha how to add two angles and subtract from 180 degrees to find the missing one. By the time the bell rang, Eva had helped three other kids solve their own problems.

As Eva packed her backpack, Tasha tapped her shoulder. "Want to sit together at lunch?" she asked. Eva grinned and nodded. She looked back at Room 14 and felt her shoulders drop. Maybe this year would not be so scary after all.

It was new seed day in Ella's class. Each child got a cup and a seed. They were planting seeds for the spring holiday. Ella dropped her seed in. Then she gasped. Her seed was upside down.

"Oh no," said Ella. "My plant will grow down into the floor."

Her teacher smiled. "Water it and wait," she said. "The seed knows what to do."

Ella watered her seed. She set it in the warm sun by the window. Every day she peeked at her cup. She even drew a monkey on the cup, because monkeys peek too.

On Friday, dirt moved. A little root came out. It grew down. Then a green shoot grew up, up toward the light.

"The root goes down first," said Ella. "Then the green part goes up. Even upside down seeds know that!"

She clapped her hands and spelled the word on her cup. "S, E, E, D. Seed!"

Emilie had promised herself she would learn to code before college, and now she was sitting on Marcus's bedroom floor surrounded by his three monitors, feeling like she had wandered into a foreign country without a map. Marcus was patient, at least. He was explaining variables for the third time when his little sister knocked and asked if they wanted pizza.

"In a minute," Marcus said, which meant he was taking this seriously. He turned back to Emilie. "Think of a variable like a container. You put a value in it, and the computer remembers where that container is. When you need the value later, you just ask for the container by name."

Emilie typed: myLocation = "home". The text appeared green on the black screen. "So the computer remembers that myLocation holds the word 'home'."

"Exactly. And if you change it later, myLocation = 'library', then now it holds 'library' instead."

She could feel the logic of it, the way things followed from other things. It was less like learning math and more like learning a language where you had to be precise about every word. She spent twenty minutes writing a program that asked for her name and then printed it back out with a greeting. When the text appeared on the screen, she felt a small, real satisfaction.

"Now let's break something," Marcus said, which was when Emilie realized he actually understood how people learned. He told her to delete a closing bracket and run the program. Error message. Error message. The red text was harsh and unhelpful. Then Marcus showed her how to read it, how the error was pointing to a place in her code, how you could follow the clues backward to find the encumbrance that was making the whole thing fail. They fixed it. The program worked again.

It was late afternoon when Marcus mentioned his hiking trip last month. He had gotten lost, or thought he had, following the map app on his phone. "It said I was in this clearing, but I was actually by the stream, like a quarter mile away. My phone was completely wrong."

Emilie was scrolling through some example code he wanted her to study. "Maybe the GPS was having an off day."

"That's what I thought. But then I read that GPS is actually crazy complicated. The satellites are moving so fast that relativity makes a real difference. Like, the satellites' clocks run fast compared to clocks on the ground. Thirty-eight microseconds a day, something like that. If nobody corrected for it, your position would be off by kilometers within a day. It's actual Einstein stuff, not just theoretical."

Emilie looked up from the screen. "Wait, so the app is using relativity?"

"Has to be. Otherwise it wouldn't work. But who thinks about that when they're just checking their phone?" He opened his laptop and found an article, and they read it together. The GPS receivers needed signals from at least four satellites. The timing had to be exact. If the satellite clocks were not corrected for relativity, the correction factor was nearly forty microseconds per day. Position errors would accumulate.

"But you were in the same place both times," Emilie said slowly. "You were lost, and the app was wrong, but relativity was working fine the whole time."

"I mean, presumably. It was my phone that had some glitch, I guess. Bad satellite geometry or something. But it made me think, you know, about all the things that have to work right for something simple to actually happen."

Emilie was quiet. She was thinking about her program, about how if she deleted one character, nothing worked until she found it and put it back. She was thinking about how the GPS satellites had to account for physics equations written down in 1905, equations about time and motion and gravity, or else people would walk in circles. She was thinking about Marcus showing her how to read an error message, following the clues to find what was wrong, how nothing could be hidden from code because code did only what you told it to do, no more and no less.

"Can you write a program that calculates position?" she asked.

Marcus laughed. "Not a real one. Not without getting into serious math. But I could show you something incipient, something basic that demonstrates the idea. You wouldn't actually sequester real GPS data, but you could fake some satellite positions and see what a receiver would have to do."

"Show me," Emilie said.

He pulled his chair closer and started typing, explaining as he went, and Emilie watched the code build up line by line, a small architecture of logic that did not care whether you understood it or believed it would work. It just worked, or it didn't.

Theo stood on his stool at the sink. He looked at his teeth in the mirror. He wanted one to fall out today.

"Look, Mom," he said. "My tooth is loose!" He pushed it with his finger. The tooth did not move.

Theo brushed his teeth. He brushed the top ones. He brushed the bottom ones. Then he showed Mom again. "Is it wiggly now?" he asked.

Mom smiled. "Your teeth are still little ones," she said. "They will get loose when you are six."

Theo made a sad face. He rinsed his mouth and spat. The water went down the drain. "But I want a big tooth now," he said.

"Let's look at a picture," said Mom. She opened a book. Theo counted the little teeth in the picture. One, two, three, all the way to twenty. He touched each one with his finger.

"So many," said Theo.

"And one day each one will fall out," said Mom. "Then bigger teeth will grow in."

Theo closed the book. He thought about big teeth. "Bigger than my thumb?" he asked.

"Bigger than your little teeth," said Mom.

Theo ran to the kitchen. He got his toothbrush from the cup. "I will brush them every day," he said. "Then they will be ready."

After lunch, Theo ate a cold ice pop. It began to melt in the sun. Drip, drip, down his hand. He licked the sweet drops and laughed.

That night, Theo brushed again. He looked in the mirror one more time. "Stay in there," he told his teeth. "Grow big and strong." Then he hopped into bed and pulled the blanket up.

Grace found the email from her mother at the kitchen table on Tuesday, printed out and circled twice in red pen. "Flights went up again. We may need to rethink the Lisbon trip." Grace read it three times, because the trip was the one thing she had been counting on since September, the tiled sidewalks, the bakery her mother swore still sold the same custard tarts as when she was fifteen. She opened the airline site herself, chose the same dates, the same seats, and watched the total climb another forty dollars while she stared at it. Nothing about the plane had changed. Same route, same hours, same little pretzels, surely.

She did what she always did when a number bothered her: she changed one thing to see what happened. In the search box she switched the currency from dollars to euros, wrote both totals on the back of her mother's email, and divided. The answer came out almost identical to what the same division would have given last month, when she had priced the trip for her grandmother. So the plane was not more expensive. Her money was buying less. She sat with that for a while, tapping the pen, feeling a bit dubious about her own arithmetic, so she ran it again with a different flight and a different date and got the same shape of answer.

Her uncle Rafael called that evening, and Grace could hear him through the wall even though her mother kept her voice low. "Three more orders this week," he was saying. "Two from Germany. One from a shop in Osaka that's never bought from us before." Uncle Rafael ran the pottery studio, mugs and bowls glazed the color of storm clouds, and for two years he had been trying, without much luck, to sell them outside the country. Now his workshop phone apparently would not stop.

At dinner Grace put the two things side by side, the way she set up problems in lab class. "Mom, if our trip costs more because our money buys less of theirs, doesn't theirs buy more of ours?" Her mother paused with her fork halfway to her mouth. "Rafael says the German buyer told him our prices finally made sense to them. Said they'd been watching them." Grace pushed her rice around her plate, testing the idea from another angle. "So the same thing that ruins our vacation is good for his business." Her mother said it sounded that way, and shrugged, and said life was full of trade like that.

Grace went upstairs and made two columns in her notebook. Column one: trip postponed, probably to next summer, maybe longer. Column two: Uncle Rafael hiring a part-time helper, his kiln running twice a week instead of once, her cousin Marta talking about a new glazing apparatus he could finally afford. It was not a fair trade, she decided, because nobody had asked her whether she wanted to make it, and there was no office to complain to, no form you could file to keep your money strong and your uncle's mugs cheap for Germans at the same time. She wrote that down too, then crossed it out, because complaining to a notebook had never once fostered anything but a sore wrist.

On Saturday she walked to the studio, where Rafael was packing mugs in newspaper, his hands gray with clay dust. "I hear we might not see Lisbon this year," he said. Grace nodded. "But you're selling to Osaka." He laughed and held up a mug, turning it so the glaze caught the light. "Want to help me wrap it? This one's going on a boat for three weeks before somebody drinks their tea out of it." She pulled a sheet of newspaper toward her and started folding.

Alicia arrived at Maya's house on Saturday afternoon to watch the soccer match, but she found her friend sprawled across the couch, still in pajamas at two o'clock.

"I can't believe you're not ready," Alicia said, dropping her backpack by the door.

Maya groaned. "My mom's been up since six. She made me take out the trash, feed the dog, and clean the kitchen. I didn't even fall asleep until midnight last night. She thinks I'm just being lazy, but I genuinely couldn't fall asleep earlier."

Alicia flopped into the armchair. "So what's your excuse for tonight? The game starts in an hour."

"I'll be ready," Maya mumbled, but she didn't move.

This wasn't the first time Alicia had noticed this pattern. Over the past few weeks, Maya had missed the bus twice and been late to lunch three times because she couldn't wake up. Her parents had started calling her irresponsible, and at school, the joke was that Maya had developed a reputation for unreliability. But Alicia had watched Maya handle group projects and help neighbors without complaint. Something else was going on.

After twenty minutes of cajoling, Maya finally dragged herself upstairs to shower. While she was gone, Alicia sat thinking. She remembered her little brother Devon falling asleep at seven every night, while their teenage cousin James never seemed tired until midnight or later. At dinner last week, her parents had been arguing about whether the high school should move its first bell from seven-thirty to eight-thirty. Her mom had said it was ridiculous to change the schedule just because teenagers wanted to sleep in. Her dad had countered that it wasn't about wanting anything arbitrary, like a preference for comfort, but something biological.

That word stuck with her now. Biological. What if teenagers were actually wired differently?

Maya returned, dressed and damp-haired, still looking exhausted. "I'm sorry," she said. "I don't know what's wrong with me."

"You're not lazy," Alicia said suddenly. "I think you literally can't fall asleep earlier. It's not about trying harder."

"What?" Maya laughed. "That makes no sense."

"Just test it," Alicia said. "Tonight, try going to bed at your usual time instead of fighting it. Don't set an alarm for tomorrow morning. See what time you naturally wake up."

Maya raised an eyebrow but nodded. "Whatever. Let's go watch the game before I miss that too."

On Monday, Maya found Alicia at lunch practically vibrating with curiosity. "I woke up at eight-fifteen," Maya announced, sitting down. "Without an alarm. And I felt actually rested."

"See?" Alicia grinned. "You weren't being lazy. Your body just works on a different schedule than your mom's."

Maya shook her head in wonder. "So what do I do about the early bus?"

"No idea yet," Alicia admitted. "But at least now we know what's actually happening."

Ella's class was learning a new dance today. Miss Chen showed them the steps. First you put your left foot forward. Then you spin around. Everyone laughed and tried it. Ella kept stepping on her own feet. "I will keep trying," she said.

At lunch, Ella planted a seed. She put it in soil upside down. Her friend Marco asked why. "The root needs to grow down first," Ella said, remembering Miss Chen's lesson. But then Ella looked worried. Her seed was planted the wrong way. Two weeks passed. Ella watered it every day. One morning something green poked up through the soil. The tiny shoot grew up toward the light. Ella's upside down seed had grown anyway. "The root found its way down," Ella whispered. She showed Marco and smiled.

Rain hammered the roof of the scout cabin, and thunder boomed so loud the windows rattled. Nicholas was stacking first aid kits with his patrol when he noticed Ben, the youngest scout, hiding under the table with his hands over his ears.

"It's okay," Nicholas said, crouching down. "Want to know a secret about that boom? Lightning heats the air around it to about 30,000 degrees Celsius. That's roughly five times hotter than the surface of the Sun." Ben peeked out with wide eyes. "The air expands so fast that it makes the boom we call thunder. So thunder is just air popping, like a giant paper bag." Nicholas had read it in a weather book twice, once out loud to his little sister, and it had persuaded her to stop hiding under blankets during storms.

Ben crawled out slowly. "Five times hotter than the Sun?" he whispered.

"Roughly five times," said Nicholas. He pointed out the window at the old water tower, their meeting landmark, visible through the gray rain. "See the tower? When lightning is far away, the boom takes longer to reach us, so it sounds soft."

Just then Maya stumbled over the scattered kits, looking awkward and embarrassed. "We should put these away together," she said.

"Good idea," said Nicholas, and he handed the smallest kit to Ben. "You're on the bandage box. That's your job."

Ben held it tight and smiled at the next rumble of thunder. "Just air popping," he said.

The argument started over a muffin, which Maika thought was ridiculous, but here she was in the library on a Saturday, tearing a page of graph paper into a hundred little squares. Her friend Dev had read a headline at breakfast, something about a poll of one thousand people, and had announced with his mouth full that it was nonsense. "A thousand people can't speak for a whole country," he'd said, crumbs flying. "There are millions of us. They just make the rest up." He hadn't meant make up the numbers, exactly, but that was how it had landed, and Maika had spent the whole walk to school wondering whether pollsters actually sat around and fabricated results, which seemed like a lot of work when you could just ask people.

The library smelled like warm dust and the lemon polish Mrs. Okafor used on the front desk, and the radiator near the window clicked in a rhythm Maika had memorized by now. She spread her hundred paper squares across the table. Each one had a letter on it. She'd labeled them in green pen, feeling the small pleasure of a plan coming together. The plan was this: Dev was due here at two o'clock, and before he arrived, she was going to run an experiment on the entire after-school crowd, which on Saturdays was maybe eighty people.

She wrote a question on the whiteboard the librarians kept for the chess club: WHICH DO YOU CHOOSE, CHOCOLATE OR VANILLA? Then, because Mrs. Okafor had once told her that asking strangers things required discretion, Maika went around quietly instead of shouting, letting each person pick a folded square from the jar without looking. That was the part she cared about, the not looking. If people chose their own squares, the ones near the top, the ones that felt lucky, it wouldn't be fair. Random was the whole point, even if she couldn't have said exactly why.

By quarter to two she had forty-two responses. Twenty-six chocolate, sixteen vanilla. She sat down and did the arithmetic twice, chewing her pencil, which her mother said was a disgusting habit and which Maika privately considered thinking gum. Then Dev arrived, dropping his backpack with a thud that earned him a look from the reading corner. "What's all this?" he said, eyeing the paper squares with the dubious expression he saved for cafeteria meatloaf and Maika's ideas.

"Your muffin argument," she said. "I counted the whole library, chocolate versus vanilla. Now watch." She swept the forty-two squares back into the jar, shook it, and drew out ten at random. Seven chocolate, three vanilla. She drew ten more. Six and four. Ten more. Eight and two, which made her wince, but the next ten came out six and four again. "It's like soup," she said, waving the jar at him. "You don't have to drink the whole pot. One spoonful tells you if it's too salty, as long as you stir first."

Dev frowned at the jar, then at her tally sheet. "So a thousand people could actually tell you about a whole country? Even a giant one?" He picked up one of the paper squares and turned it over slowly, as if the answer might be written on the back. "Same thousand either way?"

"Same thousand either way," Maika said. "City or country, it doesn't care." Dev was quiet for a moment, then grabbed a fistful of squares and stuffed them, folded and crumpled, back into the jar.

"Okay," he said, shaking it hard. "But I get to stir."

Mohamed lined up his three balls on the grass: the soccer ball, the basketball, and the tennis ball. He sorted them by size first, biggest to smallest. Then he tried sorting by bounce instead, and the order changed completely. The smallest one bounced highest. How could the littlest thing do the most? He wanted to find out if that was true for other things too, so he picked a target on the fence and started kicking.

The tennis ball was tricky. It curved when he kicked it, and it was so light that a puff of wind sent it sideways. He flinched when it zoomed back at his face, then laughed at himself. On his next kick he leaned too far, and the soccer ball smacked the fence post with a horrible CLANG, then ricocheted straight into his left ear.

Mohamed sat down hard on the grass. His ear rang like a tiny bell. What was making that sound, he wondered, when the ball was already lying in the flowerbed? Nothing was touching his ear anymore. He sat very still and listened. The ringing faded slowly, like a crystal glass humming after someone taps it and lets go. Was something inside his ear still shaking?

He ran inside and found his book about the human body. He flipped until he reached the ear page, and there it was. Sound makes your eardrum vibrate, and three tiny bones pass the vibration along into the inner ear. He stared at the picture. The bones looked like a hammer, an anvil, and a stirrup. The smallest one, the stirrup, was about the size of a grain of rice. A bone the size of rice, inside his own head, had been shaking! That was why his ear still rang after the ball was gone. The shaking took time to stop.

Back outside, he held a grain-of-rice-sized pebble next to the tennis ball. The ball was thousands of times bigger, yet the pebble was like the bone that carried the sound. Bigger was not always more important, and smaller was not always weaker. He decided to test something. He kicked the tennis ball softly at the fence, then hard, and listened to the two different clangs. Loud kick, long ring. Soft kick, short ring.

His little sister came outside and shouted his name. Mohamed put his finger to his lips. "Shhh. I'm listening to my stirrup settle down," he said, and pointed at the fence with a grin.

"Everybody knows summer is hot because we're closer to the sun," said Marcus, tapping his pencil on the desk like a judge's gavel. Mrs. Okoro had split the class into groups of four and told them to explain, on poster paper, why we have seasons. Luca's group had a sheet of blue construction paper, three markers, and a problem.

"That can't be right," Luca said slowly. He was remembering something, a half-heard fact drifting up from somewhere. "I think Earth is actually closest to the sun in early January. In winter."

Marcus laughed, but Priya stopped drawing her big yellow sun and frowned. "Then why is it cold in January?"

Luca didn't answer right away. He turned the fact over in his mind, the way he turned a puzzle piece, looking for where it might fit. If distance didn't cause the seasons, something else had to, something you couldn't see from a desk in Room 12. He pictured the globe on the shelf by the window, leaning crooked on its stand. "What if it's the tilt?" he said. "What if Earth is tilted, and the tilt is what does it?" It felt like guessing at a hidden rule, and he wanted to test it more than he wanted to be right.

He got the globe and a flashlight. "Pretend the flashlight is the sun." He held it steady while Priya spun the globe slowly, and they watched the light smear across the tilted top of the world in one position, then crowd bright and direct onto the middle in another. Marcus leaned in despite himself. "So when our part tilts away, winter," Priya said, trying to paraphrase it back. "And distance has nothing to do with it."

"Nothing," Luca said. "Weird, right? Closest and coldest at the same time."

At share-out time, Marcus stood up with the poster and did something Luca hadn't expected. "At first we thought it was distance," Marcus told the class, "because that's what everybody says in the hallway, like it's just common commerce in ideas, traded back and forth until nobody checks it. But Luca showed us it's the tilt." A couple of kids in the second row looked genuinely rattled, the way you feel when the floor shifts under a fact you thought was solid. Priya grinned at Luca across the room. "Careful," she whispered as they sat down. "You just made the whole hallway's favorite fact look kind of vulnerable."

Luca smiled and spun the globe one more time on the shelf, watching it wobble on its crooked axis.

The error message had been on her screen for forty minutes, and Madison had read it so many times it had started to look like a word in a language she didn't speak. Line 14, it said, expecting a colon. She had a colon on line 14. She had two. The girl beside her, Priya, leaned over without asking, the way people did at bootcamp after week two, when everyone's screens had become public property.

"You wrote a semicolon inside your parentheses," Priya said. "Look, right there. After the word false."

Madison looked. It was there, small and confident, exactly the kind of mistake a person makes when they are typing carefully. She deleted it, pressed run, and her program printed its greeting for the first time, plain white text on a black terminal, hello from the second loop. She sat back and felt something she didn't have a word for yet, something between relief and hunger.

They were in a converted warehouse off the bus line, thirty desks and a coffee machine that groaned like it was being robbed. The instructor, Dara, had warned them on the first day that debugging would feel like arguing with a very literal roommate. "The machine is never wrong," she had said. "It's just never generous." Madison had written that in her notebook, though she didn't yet understand it.

The project for the final week was to build a small page, any page, using the basic syntax they'd learned. Most people made portfolios. Priya was making a site for her aunt's catering business, with a form and everything. Madison had nothing, which was the problem underneath the other problems. She'd spent her savings on the bootcamp itself, six weeks of her summer before college, because she wanted to arrive in the fall already knowing how to make things. But wanting to make things was not the same as having a thing to make.

That evening, while she was procrastinating in the course's shared notes file, she found a paragraph someone had pasted in from an old article. She read it twice. The first web page had gone online in 1991 at CERN, and the inventor, Tim Berners-Lee, had persuaded the lab to release the underlying technology royalty-free in 1993. She read the second half again. Royalty-free. The whole thing, the web itself, could have been licensed, metered out, owned. She tried to imagine her mother paying a fee every time she opened a browser, the way they paid for water. It was like finding out the highway had a builder and he had decided not to put a gate on it.

She turned to Priya, who was frowning at her own screen. "Did you know the web was free on purpose?" Madison asked. "Like, someone had to decide that."

"Someone decides everything," Priya said, not looking up. "Mine's broken again. It says my closing tag is missing but I'm staring right at it."

Madison pushed her chair over. The tag was there, but it said h1 instead of h1 with the slash, a missing character the way her semicolon had been an extra one. She pointed, and Priya made a small mortified sound and fixed it. It was strange, Madison thought, how the errors were always tiny and always total. One slash and a whole page refused to exist.

She stayed late, long after Priya caught her bus, building a page about the decision she'd found. She titled it "1991" and wrote three short paragraphs: the page at CERN, the release two years later, and then her own question at the bottom, in the footer she'd spent an hour learning to style: "Would you have made it free?" She added a text box so a visitor could answer. It didn't save anyone's answer anywhere, because she hadn't learned databases yet, and there was something honest in that, a question asked aloud with no way to record the reply.

When Dara came by to lock up, she paused behind Madison's chair. "Nice footer," she said. "Is the box real?"

"It writes to nowhere," Madison said. "I only know how to make the front of things so far."

"That's how everyone starts," Dara said, and it didn't sound like a line. She waited while Madison saved her files, and outside the night had cooled enough that the walk to the bus stop felt like something earned. Her phone buzzed with a message from Priya: found three more missing slashes, this language is a scam. Madison typed back, "the web itself is free though," and put the phone in her pocket, laughing at what she imagined Priya's face would do when she read it.

Grace sat at the library's corner table with her colored pencils spread across a sheet of kraft paper, sketching the distribution of shadows cast by the afternoon sun through the tall windows. She had volunteered to create visualizations for the school's diversity report, a project that had seemed straightforward until she began arranging the data into charts. The report extolled the admissions office's success: overall, the school had admitted forty-eight percent women and fifty-two percent women from the applicant pool. The numbers looked balanced, fair even, so she'd started with a simple bar chart, thinking it would take an afternoon.

But something about the result bothered her. She set down her pencils and pulled out the spreadsheet on her laptop, scrolling through the departmental breakdowns. The engineering program showed fifty-six percent women admitted compared to forty-four percent of women applicants. The arts program admitted sixty-two percent of women applicants and only forty percent of men. Physics, chemistry, biology all followed similar patterns, each department admitting women at rates equal to or higher than their proportion among applicants. She frowned, moving back to the overall figure. How could each individual program show near parity or favor women while the total reversed itself?

"You look confused," Marcus said, pulling up a chair. He was working on the report too, handling the written components. "Everything okay?"

"The numbers don't match," Grace said, turning her laptop toward him. "Look at every department. Women are doing better or the same. But overall, we supposedly admitted fewer women."

Marcus leaned in, studying the data. "Maybe the data's wrong."

"I checked it three times." She moved through the spreadsheet again, pointing at each line. "Engineering, forty-eight applicants total, twenty-seven women. They took fourteen of the women. Arts, ninety-two applicants, sixty-five women, took forty of them. Biology, fifty-eight applicants, thirty-four women, took twenty-one. Every single one." She sat back. "This shouldn't be possible."

"What if more women applied to the harder programs?" Marcus suggested. "The ones that reject everyone."

Grace opened another sheet. Applied engineering: one hundred fifty applicants, fifty-four women. Applied mathematics: one hundred eighty applicants, only thirty-one women. The pattern emerged like a photograph developing. Women had concentrated their applications in the programs with the most selective admissions, the ones where nearly everyone, regardless of gender, was turned away. Men had scattered across programs that accepted broader cohorts. The math was suddenly legible: within each program, the admissions office had treated applicants equitably, yet the uneven distribution of applications created an aggregate effect that made the entire system appear skewed.

"So the office isn't doing anything wrong," Marcus said slowly.

"That's not what this shows," Grace replied, picking up a pencil again. She began sketching two side by side visualizations, one showing the raw overall percentages and the other breaking them down by program. "It shows that when you look at the whole thing together, you get one story. When you look at the pieces, you get another. Both are true. They're just not the same truth."

She shaded in the differences between her sketches, the visual contrast making the contradiction clear without resolving it. The admissions office could point to their departmental numbers with genuine pride. The overall statistics were still accurate. What she was creating wasn't proof of bias or proof of fairness, only a map of how the same data could tell different stories depending on how you arranged it. She understood now why the project had felt incomplete. The pragmatism of a conciliatory visualization wouldn't actually settle anything; it would only show the question itself more clearly.

"Are you going to tell them?" Marcus asked.

Grace looked at her sketches, then at him. "I'm going to show them this. What they do with it is something else."

Theo wiggled his bottom tooth at breakfast. "Will it fall out today?" he asked Mom. Mom smiled and kept making toast. Theo pulled harder on the tooth. It did not come loose yet. He felt sad about waiting.

At the sink, Mom showed him his toothbrush. "Let's clean your teeth now," she said. Theo brushed the top ones first. Then he brushed the bottom ones too. He saw something in the mirror. One tooth looked a little wiggly. "That one moves!" Theo said with wonder.

Mom nodded. "You have twenty teeth right now," she said. "When you get bigger, some will fall out. Then new bigger teeth will grow in." Theo looked at his teeth again. He stopped pulling and just brushed gently instead.

That night at dinner, Theo bit into an apple. His loose tooth wiggled but stayed put. "It will come out when it is ready," he told himself. He smiled at Mom, showing all his teeth.

The first thing Parker did on the first day of his senior year was drop his schedule into the fountain. Not intentionally. He had been juggling his phone, a granola bar, and the folded paper with his locker combination written on the back, and the schedule simply chose freedom. He watched it float, the ink already bleeding, and thought about how his grandfather claimed to have survived entire decades without knowing where he was supposed to be at any given hour.

The second thing he did was walk into AP History four minutes late, which mattered, because Ms. Okafor locked the door at the bell and made latecomers sing the chorus of a song of her choosing. Parker had escaped this ritual for three years. Today he sang " MMMBop," solo, while thirty classmates filmed it. A boy in the second row, a new kid with a lanyard still creased from the packaging, laughed so hard he knocked his own phone off his desk.

"Sorry," the new kid said afterward, in the hall. "I'm Desh. That was the greatest thing I've ever witnessed, and I once saw a swan fight a groom."

Parker decided he liked him. They had study hall together next, which was really an hour of supervised anarchy in the library, and Desh immediately litigated the seating chart like a man defending a mansion. "This is my table now," he told a sophomore, with tremendous politeness. "I'll allow visitation."

The argument that got going, though, the one that ate the whole hour, started when Desh pulled up a photo on his phone. "Look at this. My uncle sent it. A phone ad from the eighties." It showed a brick with a rubber antenna, squat and triumphant, like a walkie-talkie that had been lifting weights. "Four thousand dollars," Desh said. "Nearly four thousand, in eighties money. For that."

"You're making it up," Parker said.

"Am not. And that's the consumer version, the one regular people could buy. Ten years before that, the first cell phone call ever was made on a prototype, and the thing weighed over a kilogram. One point one kilograms. A guy held that up to his head, in public, and made a call, and that was the beginning."

Parker did the math on his phone, which weighed less than the granola bar in his pocket. He held the phone in one hand and imagined a bag of sugar plus a little more in the other, pressed against his ear. He thought of his grandfather again, who narrated the past in a turgid, ceremonial way, every sentence about the old days arriving draped in velvet. "Back then a phone was furniture," he liked to say, meaning the rotary in the hallway. But this was stranger than furniture. This was a luxury object, a car-payment object, a device that said something about you the moment you lifted it.

"Okay, but here's my question," Parker said. "Was that thing amazing or terrible? Because my grandfather says new technology is ruining everyone's attention span, and he tells it like the past was pure and the present is a fall. But he also complains that he couldn't call anyone from anywhere until he was fifty."

"That's revisionist," Desh said. "He's editing. Nobody's memory is the whole movie."

"No, he's not lying, exactly. He's just choosing." Parker turned his phone over in his hand. Both things were true, he decided, or at least both things were honestly held: the brick was an absurd luxury, and it was also a door, and standing on either side of it you could tell a different story about what people lost or gained when it opened. He could not make the two stories into one, and he suspected that was fine, or at least that pretending otherwise would be worse. "I think you can hold both," he said. "I think you have to, actually, or you end up either worshiping the past or trashing it, and both of those are boring."

"You should put that in your college essay," Desh said. " 'I hold both.' They'll weep."

"They'll reject me for excessive wisdom." Parker tucked his phone away, and they headed for the cafeteria, where the line was already thirty students deep and a rumor was spreading that the new vending machine gave two drinks for the price of one if you unplugged it first.

"Should we litigate the lunch line," Desh asked, "or commit a felony?"

Parker looked at the machine, glowing and patient, and then at the librarian, who was watching them with the flat gaze of a woman who had heard the rumor too. "Unplug it," he said.

Natalie had rewritten the line four times before Mr. Okafor even came around, and each version failed in a different way. The assignment was simple on paper: a program that took a list of names and counted how many times each one appeared. She could do it. She had done it. The problem was that her program kept telling her the answer was zero.

"You're comparing the whole string instead of the piece," said Desi, leaning over from the next station in the school's cramped computer lab, where the radiators clanked and the afternoon light came in sideways. Desi was generous with help in a way that made Natalie feel both grateful and slightly smaller, like being handed something she should have carried herself.

"I know," Natalie said. "I fixed that. Now it just... doesn't run."

"Then read the error."

"Reading the error feels like admitting I don't know anything."

"Everyone's an acolyte at something," Desi said. "You should see me in ceramics."

Natalie laughed despite herself, and then, because there was nothing else to do, she read the error. Missing colon. Line fourteen. A single mark the width of a fingernail, and the whole machine had refused her on principle. She added it, ran the program, and watched the names scroll past with their counts, ordinary as weather.

The list she had fed it was not the assignment list. It was her follower list, exported that morning after a conversation she kept replaying. Her cousin Priya, home from her first semester of college, had scrolled Natalie's profile on the couch and said, "A thousand people, Nat. Who do you actually call?" It had sounded like an accusation, and Natalie had answered with something sullen and short, and Priya had gone to bed early.

The program counted. She had written a second part herself, past the assignment's edge: for every name, check whether it appeared in her messages that month. The output was a short list, so short she counted it twice on screen, then on her fingers under the desk. Eleven names. She sat with that for a while, the radiator ticking, Desi debugging something three seats over, murmuring at her screen like it was a stubborn friend.

Priya had left a library book on the coffee table, face down, a chapter marked with a receipt. Natalie had picked it up that morning looking for something to be annoyed at and found instead a page about an anthropologist, Robin Dunbar, and a figure she kept turning over: roughly 150 stable relationships, the number humans can actually maintain. Priya had underlined it, and in the margin, in her terrible handwriting, had written, "so a thousand isn't a betrayal of friendship, it's a different thing entirely." That was the part Natalie couldn't stop thinking about. She had been treating the thousand like a lie, proof she was hollow, when maybe it was just a different category, like the difference between a name in a list and a name with a count beside it.

She tried to historicize her own shame, the way her sociology teacher was always pushing: what had made her generation measure worth in numbers at all? But that line of thinking dissolved when she looked at the eleven. Whatever the era, those eleven were hers, and she had not called Priya back since September, and Priya had still left a book open for her on the table like an invitation.

"Hey, Desi," she said. "Can a program text someone?"

"Only if you write the code for it and I don't think Mr. Okafor wants us calling APIs on the school network."

"I'll use my phone, obviously."

She typed the message standing at the window, where the lacrosse team was dragging cones across the mud. "Found your book. Also wrote a program about it. Kind of. Can I call tonight?" Then, because Priya deserved specifics: "I have a list. You're on it. You're near the top."

Her phone buzzed before she'd put it down. "Near the top?"

The lab was emptying, chairs scraping, Desi waving on her way out. Natalie looked at her screen one more time, at the eleven names with their small honest counts, then typed back with her thumb.

"Okay. The top. Eleven people, Priya. You're one of them. That's the whole output."

Alicia was on the third quarter of the Celtics game when her grandfather shuffled into the living room with his laptop and a cup of coffee that smelled like burnt almonds, the kitchen's usual morning mistake. He settled into his chair with a groan and opened the screen, squinting at something that made him frown in that particular way that meant he was reading news, not the sports scores Alicia was watching.

"Your mother called," he said without looking away. "She's worried about your chemistry exam next week."

Alicia made a noncommittal sound. Chemistry had always come easily to her, so she'd done what made sense: she'd spent the last three days cramming everything, eight hours yesterday alone, sitting at her desk with her notes and her periodic table and her will to retain it all before test day. It was efficient. It was focused. It should work.

"She said your cousin Marcos did something different," her grandfather continued, finally looking at her. "He's been studying for his accounting certification for weeks now, just an hour or two each day. She mentioned it because he passed the first time, and his brother studied for two weeks straight and failed."

Alicia shrugged, but something about this bothered her. Marcos was smart, but not anomalously so. His brother was just as capable. She'd seen them both struggle through their teenage years with the same kinds of problems everyone else did. There was no obvious reason why one would pass and one would fail based on raw ability alone.

The Celtics scored. The crowd roared through the television speakers. Alicia watched the replay, but her attention was divided now, split between the screen and the question forming in her mind. She could argue that maybe Marcos just cared more about accounting, had more motivation, more reasons to pay attention. That would vindicate the idea that hours were all that mattered, that effort was straightforward in the way a chemical equation was straightforward: more reactants equals more product. But his brother had tried hard too. She'd heard him complain about it.

"Did Marcos say why he spread it out like that?" she asked.

Her grandfather shook his head. "I think that's just how he found he could manage with his job. But he got the highest score in his section."

Alicia picked up her phone and searched. It took her only a few minutes to find the articles, the studies going back more than a century, all saying essentially the same thing in different words: spacing study sessions over days produced better long-term memory than the same total time crammed into one session. The research was old and it was consistent. Ebbinghaus had documented it all the way back in eighteen eighty-five. The evidence was there, not in her grandmother's favorite memento cookbook or some motivational poster, but in actual data.

She thought about her eight-hour Saturday, how alert she'd been in the first hour and how her brain felt like warm sludge by hour seven, how the information had seemed to slide through her mind like water. She thought about Marcos spreading his studying across weeks, probably reviewing some material multiple times, her brain encountering the same concepts from different angles, in different contexts, with time for something to settle between sessions.

Her grandfather was watching her now, waiting for some kind of response. The game continued mutely beneath their quiet. There was a reciprocal relationship here that she hadn't considered: the spacing and the retention, how they fed into each other in ways that simple hours couldn't explain.

"I need to study differently," Alicia said, and she reached for her chemistry notes.

Zachary had a big week ahead. On Monday his music teacher announced that the whole third grade would learn to read real sheet music, and on Friday there would be an eclipse. Two amazing things in five days!

Reading music was trickier than Zachary expected. The notes on the staff were not just high or low, and not just on lines or in spaces. They were both at once. He sorted his flashcards into piles: notes on lines that were high, notes on lines that were low, notes in spaces that were high, notes in spaces that were low. Four piles, and every note belonged in exactly one. "I get it!" he told his friend Amira. "A note can be low and on a line, or high and in a space. I have to look at two things at the same time." His fingers felt clumsy on the recorder at first, but he kept practicing until they grew flexible enough to hop from hole to hole.

Then Friday came, and the principal said no one could look at the sun. Not even a peek. Zachary's class had made dark boxes with one tiny hole, and he carried his outside like treasure. His grandfather, an immigrant who had built things his whole life, had helped him tape the foil just right.

Zachary pointed the little hole at the sun. On the far wall inside the box, a small round picture appeared, and it was upside down! The crowd of kids had to retreat inside when clouds passed, but the picture came back, and slowly the round shape turned into a crescent.

"Upside down and shrinking," Zachary whispered. "Look, look, look!"

Marcus had two part-time jobs that summer, stocking shelves at Halloran's Grocery on weekdays and answering the phone at a small gear shop called Trailhead on Saturdays, and it was at Trailhead that the argument about water began. His boss, Ms. Okafor, had him read the customer emails each morning and draft replies in the shop's standard format: a greeting, a clear answer to the question, a proposed solution, and a courteous close. He was clumsy at it the first few weeks, and she kept sending drafts back with notes like "good structure, tighten the second paragraph," which stung less than he expected, because she also wrote "this is much better than your last one" every single time.

On the Saturday in question, an email arrived from a man named Mr. Reyes, who wanted a refund for a water filter he had bought three weeks earlier, and attached a long, angry account of a day hike that had gone wrong. Marcus read it twice. Then Dan, the senior clerk, read over his shoulder and said, "Deny it. He used the filter. Look at the photos, it's scratched to hell."

Marcus drafted the denial, but something in it bothered him, and instead of sending it he printed Mr. Reyes's account and took it to the break room. The story was this: Mr. Reyes had run out of water on a ridge trail, gotten turned around, and met another hiker coming down who had one bottle left. He had offered the man forty dollars for it, then, when the man hesitated, the silver ring off his own finger. The stranger had taken the ring and given him the water, and Mr. Reyes, who was shaken and felt the world had shown him something ugly about people, now wanted Trailhead to refund the filter he blamed for the whole ordeal, because it had "failed him when he needed it most."

"His whole theory is that the ring proves the stranger was a vulture," Dan said later, leaning on the counter. "Guy was probably impetuous, offered the ring before the guy even asked for anything, and now he's embarrassed."

"Or the stranger just took advantage," Marcus said. He liked that Dan's version made Mr. Reyes the author of his own misfortune, but he could not make it fit the photos. He scrolled through them again: the filter's intake hose was split lengthwise, a clean manufacturing crack, not the kind of damage a careless week of use would leave. "The filter actually broke, Dan. He's wrong about people being vultures, maybe, but he's right about the filter." The two explanations were tangled together in Mr. Reyes's mind, and in Dan's, and Marcus could see that the argument about the stranger was doing all the emotional work while the evidence sat there untouched, split hose and all.

He went back to the break room and looked at the ring sentence for a long time. He kept thinking that the stranger's behavior needed explaining, and then, slowly, that maybe it didn't, or not the way Mr. Reyes thought. Water at the shop cost a dollar a liter and sat in pallets by the register; nobody would trade a ring for a bottle in the parking lot. On the ridge, one bottle had apparently been worth a ring to a man who was stranded. Marcus did not fully know what to do with that, except that it seemed to cut against the idea that the stranger was a vulture. It seemed to suggest that the same water could be worth almost nothing in one place and everything in another, depending on the situation of the person holding it. He could not prove what the stranger had been thinking, he decided; the trade was consistent with greed and with something else, and the photos said nothing either way about a man's soul. What the photos did show was a cracked hose.

He drafted a new reply. It offered a full refund plus a replacement hose, apologized for the equipment failure in plain professional language, and, after some hesitation, included one careful sentence: "It sounds like a frightening day, and we're glad someone was there with water when you needed it." He showed it to Dan first. "It's a reconciliation offer," Marcus said. "We're not saying he was right about the guy with the ring, and we're not saying he was wrong. The filter's the part we can actually fix."

Dan read it, shrugged, and said, "Better than the denial. Send it." Ms. Okafor forwarded Marcus's draft back an hour later with only one addition, a line about a discount on his next purchase, and a note at the bottom: "You worked this one out yourself. Keep arguing with the first draft like that."

Monday morning, before his shift at Halloran's, Marcus checked the shop's inbox from his phone. Mr. Reyes had replied. The message was short and formal, thanking them for the replacement, and then, in a separate paragraph that broke the format entirely, he wrote that he had mailed the ring back to the stranger's address, which he had gotten from the trailhead register, with a note enclosed. He did not say what the note said, and Marcus, walking in past the pallet of bottled water by the register, caught himself wondering about it all through the first hour of stocking shelves.

Emilie had promised herself she would learn to code before September, and now it was the last week of August and she was sitting on Rosa's bedroom floor with a laptop that kept telling her, in polite orange text, that something was wrong on line 4. Rosa was making tea downstairs, which meant Emilie was alone with the error, which meant the error was winning.

She had come over intending to build the small thing they had agreed on: a program that took three map coordinates and told you how far apart they were. Rosa wanted it for planning hikes, and Emilie wanted, more than anything she could say out loud, to be the kind of person who could make a thing like that work. Line 4 was supposed to turn a string of numbers into something the program could do math with. Instead the program did nothing, or worse than nothing, it did something obviously insane, announcing that two points half a kilometer apart were separated by 11,000 kilometers.

"You're making that face," Rosa said from the doorway, holding two mugs and watching Emilie stare at the screen as if it had insulted her family.

"I'm making the face of a person who has been defeated by punctuation." Emilie turned the laptop so Rosa could see. "Look. I copied it exactly. Semi-semicolon, curly brace, the whole encumbrance."

Rosa set down the mugs and folded herself onto the rug. "Okay, but copied from where?"

"From a tutorial. And then I changed a part I thought I understood." That was the humiliating truth of it: the mistake was not mysterious. Emilie had seen lat and lon in two different orders in two different examples and had chosen, with total confidence, the wrong one. When she swapped them, the distance collapsed from absurd to correct, and she laughed so suddenly that tea nearly went into the keyboard. "That's it. That was the whole bug. I gave it the coordinates backwards."

"Eleven thousand kilometers for a typo," Rosa said. "I want you to remember that number."

They worked for another hour, and the program grew a loop, then a list of points, then a way to add a point by typing it in. Emilie began to feel the incipient pleasure of competence, the cautious kind, the kind you don't trust on the first day. Then Rosa asked the question that changed the shape of the afternoon. "So this is basically what my phone does, right? Same math?"

"Sort of," Emilie said, and then stopped, because she actually did not know. Her phone did not know where it was by dead reckoning or by her typing coordinates in backwards. It listened to the sky. She searched on Rosa's desktop, half to avoid more coding and half because the question had gotten its hooks in her, and found herself reading about receivers and satellites, and then about clocks, and then about Einstein, and then she read the same paragraph twice because she did not believe it the first time.

The satellites' clocks, if nobody corrected them, would run about 38 microseconds a day fast relative to clocks on the ground, and without the correction, position errors would grow by kilometers each day. Kilometers. Every day. Emilie read it aloud, slowly, and watched Rosa's expression do the same thing her own had done. "So when I check the map app on a trail," Rosa said, "Einstein is in there somewhere."

"Apparently Einstein is in there whether you invite him or not." Emilie leaned back against the bed. There was something in this she could not stop turning over. She had spent the afternoon believing that code was the layer that mattered, that if you got the syntax right the machine would tell you the truth. But underneath her thirty lines of borrowed arithmetic was a system that timed signals from at least four satellites, and underneath that was physics that nobody at the keyboard ever thinks about, and if the people who built it had skipped one correction, Rosa's phone would have put the trailhead in the next county by Friday. Being right, Emilie understood, was less a single act than a whole stack of people being right, all the way down.

And yet the typo had still mattered. Swap two words and you get eleven thousand kilometers of your own making. So it was both. The careful correction in the satellites and the careful order of the variables on line 4, and she could not honestly say which one was more fundamental, only that both had to hold for Rosa to find her way up a mountain.

"Say something wise," Rosa said. "You have the face again."

"I have a smaller face this time. It's the face of someone who checked something." Emilie pulled the laptop back and, mostly to prove she could, wrote a comment on line 4: lat before lon, always. She had to sequester that rule somewhere or it would escape by Thursday. Then she typed a new pair of coordinates, ones for the trailhead Rosa kept talking about, and ran the program.

"Two kilometers to the ridge," Rosa said, reading over her shoulder. "That's not 11,000."

"That's not 11,000," Emilie agreed, and saved the file.

Alexander stood in the bathroom doorway watching his mother organize the cabinet under the sink, her hands moving with practiced efficiency among bottles and tubes he had never really examined. She glanced up at him with an expression that suggested she had been waiting for this conversation.

"Your dermatologist mentioned something when you were in last week," she said, setting down a container of face wash. "About your routine. I should have talked to you about it sooner, but I wasn't sure how to start."

He felt his shoulders tense. At sixteen, he had developed a presentiment that any discussion about his skin or hygiene carried an implicit criticism, a suggestion that he was doing something wrong. He had been washing his face in the morning and before bed for years. What more could there be?

His mother pulled out a small bottle filled with clear liquid. "This is a toner. And this one here is a moisturizer with SPF." She held them at eye level as though their properties might become obvious through proximity. "The thing is, your skin needs different things on different days. If you've had breakouts five days in a row, you might think that on the sixth day it's guaranteed to clear up because your luck has to turn around. But that's not really how it works."

Alexander frowned. "That doesn't make sense. If something keeps happening, shouldn't it stop eventually?"

"That's what feels true," she said, setting the bottles on the counter. "But each day your skin is its own situation. What you did yesterday doesn't make today more or less likely to have breakouts. The breakouts yesterday don't create a debt that today has to pay off by being clear."

He picked up the toner, reading the label without taking in the words. Something in her explanation bothered him, though he couldn't articulate why. It seemed to suggest a kind of randomness to his own body, a place where his effort and intention couldn't guarantee outcomes. Yet he had always assumed that if he just found the right routine and stuck to it, everything would improve. The extrinsic factors, the humidity and stress and sleep, were variables he couldn't control. What he could control was showing up with consistency.

"So what's the point of doing anything if it doesn't make a difference?" he asked.

His mother took the toner from his hands and unscrewed the cap. "That's not what I'm saying. It's that we can't make the results come on our schedule just by believing they're overdue. You use the toner and moisturizer not because they guarantee clear skin tomorrow, but because they're good for your skin today. And over time, good habits do matter. But not in the way you think." She demonstrated the proper way to apply it with a cotton pad, dabbing gently rather than rubbing. "Watch how you do this. Really watch."

Over the next week, Alexander began to reify what his mother had suggested by actually paying attention to what he was doing. He stopped rushing through his routine while thinking about other things. He applied each product as it was meant to be applied. He noticed that some mornings his skin looked better and some mornings it looked worse, and that neither outcome felt like a punishment or reward for yesterday's efforts. The inconsistency was simply there, independent of what he wanted or expected.

By the second week, he found himself reaching for the toner without being reminded, not because he believed it would erase the breakout he had woken up to, but because the routine itself had become something quieter than hope. It was care, directed at himself in a way that didn't require the guarantee of immediate results.

His mother passed by the bathroom one morning and saw him at the sink, taking his time with the small ritual. She smiled but said nothing, which felt like the right choice.

Everett sat high in the big sports arena. He watched the players move up and down the ice. It was lunchtime, and Dad handed him a cupcake with white frosting.

Everett turned around to wave at a friend. Then he looked back. Someone had poked a finger in his frosting! There was a little dent on top.

Everett looked at the dent very closely. He could see tiny lines in the frosting. They looked like the tiny lines on his own fingertips. Dad said those lines are fingerprints. No two people have the same fingerprints, not even twins. So the mark was not from Everett's finger.

Everett looked at his little sister, Kit. Her fingers were white with frosting. "It was you," Everett said. Kit giggled and licked her thumb. Then Dad gave Everett a new cupcake, and the slippery ice below shined bright under the lights.

Thomas had joined the robotics club for the robots, not the money, but somebody had to count the pizza fund, and after Mrs. Okafor looked around the room with raised eyebrows, he had raised his hand. Now he sat in the corner of the lab every Tuesday with a battered cash box and a spiral notebook, which was why Priya came to him after practice, holding her phone like it had bitten her.

"Can I show you something and you promise not to laugh?" she said. She had turned eighteen that month, and to celebrate, her sister had added her as an authorized user on a credit card so Priya could buy the parts for the regional build, a thousand dollars of motors and aluminum that the school would never cover. "I'm being responsible. I pay them every single month. Twenty-five dollars, right on time. And the balance barely moves. Am I doing the math wrong, or is the math evil?"

Thomas took the phone and found the statement buried under three confirmation emails about servo orders, because Priya's inbox was a torrential flood of shipping notices that she never deleted. He read the line about interest, then the line about the balance, then he read them again. He pulled his notebook toward him, the one with the club budget, and flipped past the pizza ledger to a blank page. "Okay," he said slowly. "Don't panic. But at twenty-five a month, this takes like five and a half years to pay off. And the interest on top, over six hundred dollars." Priya made a sound like a kettle. "Six hundred? I could buy a whole second robot for six hundred dollars. A bad robot, but still."

He wasn't sure he believed it himself, so he did what he always did with numbers that seemed wrong: he changed one thing and watched what happened. On the page he wrote 25 and traced the balance down, month after month, the line crawling like an ant. Then, out of pure curiosity, he crossed it out and wrote 100. The years collapsed. He sat back, genuinely startled that a single decision, made once, at a kitchen table, with a phone, could reach five years into the future and grab somebody by the wallet. He thought about how he'd spent his own savings on a model kit he'd built once and shelved, and how that at least had been a one-time mistake, not one that charged him rent to keep existing.
