Priya watched his pencil oscillate between the two columns like it couldn't decide which future to point at. "My sister said just pay the minimum," she said, with the flat deference of someone repeating the wisdom of an older sibling she was beginning to suspect was an idiot. "She said that's what the card is for."

"Your sister," Thomas said, "has never once balanced the pizza fund." He tore the page out, folded it into a paper airplane, and sailed it across the lab to where she sat. She caught it, unfolded it, and stared at the two columns for a long moment, then at her phone, then at him. "Okay," she said. "New plan. I pay a hundred a month, I finish paying by the time I graduate, and you get first slice of pizza for the rest of the year." Thomas held out his hand, and she shook it, solemn as a treaty. "Deal," he said, and wrote it in the ledger, under Serrano, P., debts of honor, pizza obligations, paid in full.

Beatrice went on a picnic with Grandma. She held Grandma's hand in the parking lot. The sun made the benches hot. "Careful, that bench is hot," said Grandma. Beatrice touched the cool grass instead. They sat by a blue pond. It was quiet there. Then Beatrice heard a noise. Grrr. It came from her middle. "Grandma, something is in there!" "Was it your tummy?" Beatrice put her hand on her tummy. She waited. Grrr. It growled again. She did wonder what made the sound. Her tummy was empty, and it made noise. "I am hungry," she said. Grandma opened the basket. Beatrice wanted to touch the shiny knife. "No, that is not for you," said Grandma. Beatrice ate a sandwich instead. Grrr went Ben's tummy, the dog. "Ben is hungry too," said Beatrice. She tossed him a small piece of bread.

Alexander sat in the back row of the seminar room, watching Mr. Chen hand back the first debate assignment of the year. The stack of papers moved forward one by one, and when Alexander finally received his, he saw the grade circled in red at the top: ninety-two percent. He felt his shoulders relax. He had worked hard on that argument about whether social media companies should be regulated, and the effort had paid off.

Two weeks later, the second debate assignment was due. This time Alexander felt confident enough to prepare less carefully. He still had aptitude for this kind of thinking, he reasoned. The arguments came naturally to him. He spent half the time he had spent before, throwing together ideas about whether school uniforms improved behavior. When Mr. Chen returned the papers, Alexander's stomach tightened. Eighty-four percent. He turned the paper over, confused, looking for notes that might explain the drop. The comment simply said, "Less developed reasoning. Rushed."

That night, Alexander sat at his desk thinking about what had changed. He had not suddenly become worse at debate. His brain had not lost its ability to construct an argument overnight. Something else was happening, though he could not quite name it. He decided to test something. For the third assignment, he would immerse himself in the work completely, giving it even more attention than the first one. He would write and rewrite, testing every claim, considering every counterargument. He wanted to see if more effort would bring back that ninety-two.

The third paper came back marked ninety percent. Close to the first score, certainly higher than the second, but not quite the same. Alexander stared at it, then pulled out his previous papers and arranged them in order. Ninety-two, eighty-four, ninety. The pattern bothered him because it did not make complete sense. He had done the most work for the third assignment, yet it did not earn the highest score. His second attempt, the rushed one, had been the worst. But something nagged at him: if he had done so poorly on the second one, why had he improved on the third without doing anything particularly special, just returning to his normal level of effort?

During the fourth seminar, Mr. Chen asked the class to think about why some experiments produced extreme results. A student named Maria raised her hand. "Maybe the extreme result was just luck," she said. "And then regular luck happens the next time instead." Alexander's head came up. That was it. Not luck exactly, but something like it. His first paper had been unusually good, and his second had been unusually bad. He had assumed the second paper proved something was wrong with him. But what if his first paper had just been better than his typical work, and his second had been worse? His third paper might not be proving that he was improving his recovery. It might just be his ordinary self showing up again.

He raised his hand before he could second-guess himself. "What if the first result is just an outlier?" he asked carefully. "Like, what if someone does really well one time by chance, and then the next time they just do normal, but they think something changed in them?"

Mr. Chen nodded slowly. "That is worth examining," he said. "What would tell you the difference?"

Alexander thought about his three papers spread across his desk at home. "You would need to see what happens over a long time," he said. "Not just two tests in a row."

Maria leaned forward, considering this. "So maybe the reason didn't change," she said. "The performance just went back to normal."

"Exactly," Alexander said, and he felt something settle in him, something like understanding.

Declan stood at his friend Marcus's kitchen counter, staring at the recipe card for homemade pasta sauce. Marcus's mom had left them to make lunch, which meant Declan would finally learn something he'd been wanting to try. He measured out tomatoes, garlic, and olive oil, feeling the smooth glass of the measuring cup in his palm.

"Why do we have to follow this exactly?" Declan asked, reading aloud. The recipe said to add salt before tasting, but he didn't understand the point of that order. Marcus shrugged, so Declan decided to do it his own way. He tasted the sauce first, found it bland, and threw in a big pinch of salt. The tomato flavor still seemed flat and lifeless, like something was missing. He added more salt, then more, chasing that bright taste he wanted.

"Okay, it's ready," he announced, but when Marcus tasted it, he made a face. "Dude, that's basically brine," Marcus said, handing the spoon back. Declan tried it again and realized Marcus was right. The salt had made everything harsh and corrosive to his tongue, burning instead of helping. He felt the familiar sting of getting it wrong.

That's when Marcus showed him something. He poured the sauce into a clear glass bowl and held it up to the window. In the bright sunlight, Declan could see the red tomatoes suspended in the liquid oil. "My dad told me something weird," Marcus said. "He was fishing once and kept missing fish he could clearly see. Turns out the light bends when it goes through water, so a fish under the surface appears shallower and closer than it really is. You have to aim below where it seems to be." Marcus looked at the sauce in the glass. "I wonder if that's why the salt tasted wrong to you. You saw the problem on top, but maybe the real problem was hiding deeper in how the flavors work together."

Declan studied the mixture, thinking about invisible things changing what you see. He grabbed a fresh can of tomatoes from the pantry. This time, he followed the recipe exactly, trusting the steps he couldn't understand yet. When he tasted it at the end, the salt brought out sweetness and depth instead of harshness. "That's better," he said, and Marcus nodded.

The flyer had said "Intro to Coding, Thursdays, Riverside Community Center, free," and Isabelle had read the word free twice, because free was the whole reason she was there. The college she was starting in the fall had emailed her a list of things she could do to prepare, and a laptop she could not yet afford, and a tuition statement she had read standing up so she would not have to sit with it. So here she was, seven weeks before move-in, in a room smelling of chlorine from the pool down the hall, taking the last seat at a table of ancient desktops.

The instructor, a grad student named Priya who wore a lanyard covered in enamel pins, wrote print("hello") on the whiteboard and told them to type it exactly. Isabelle typed it, hit run, and when hello appeared in the black rectangle at the bottom of the screen she actually laughed out loud. A boy across the table glanced over. "Sorry," she whispered. "It just did what I said." She had spent seventeen years doing what other people said, and this was the first time the direction had run the other way.

The problem was the assignment for the summer showcase. Priya wanted each of them to build something small but real by the last Thursday, a page or a program, and Isabelle knew exactly what she wanted: a website for her grandmother's meals-on-wheels route. Grandma Rose delivered to eleven housebound neighbors every Wednesday, tracking them on a paper map with pencil marks, and twice this year someone had been missed. A page where clients could check a box, where Rose could see the day's route, that was the want that drove everything.

Except by week three, the want had run into the wall. Isabelle's plan involved buttons that stored information, and every time she followed a tutorial her code came back with a red bar of errors, a cascade of accusing text that seemed personally disappointed in her. Priya taught them the word for it, debugging, and taught them the method: read the first error, not the last; change one thing; run it again. Isabelle stayed after class in the emptying room, hunched over a loop that would not loop, and felt the incipient headache of someone who has been staring at the same twelve lines for forty minutes.

The boy from across the table, Marcus, was always there late too. He was building a game about a frog, badly and joyfully, and he talked while he worked, a running commentary that should have been annoying and somehow wasn't. That night he leaned over at her screen. "You closed the quote late. Line nine. See?" She found it, a single quotation mark sitting one character to the right of where it belonged, deleted it, retyped it, ran the program, and the box appeared. She raised both fists over her head like a referee calling a touchdown, and Marcus laughed so hard the woman at the front desk shushed them.

That was the night he told her the thing, the thing that rearranged something in her head. He was reading off a crumpled printout for a history project, half to himself. "The first web page went online in 1991 at CERN," he recited, "and the inventor, Tim Berners-Lee, persuaded the lab to release the underlying technology royalty-free in 1993." He said royalty-free twice, frowning at it, and then shrugged and went back to his frog.

Isabelle did not go back to her loop. She sat with the words. She looked at the screen in front of her, the black rectangle and the hello she had made it say, and understood, slowly and then all at once, that the whole thing she was learning could have been a product. Somebody had owned it. It could have been sold to her the way textbooks were sold to her, the way the meal plan was sold to her, access metered out in subscriptions, and instead it had been let go, handed to everyone at once, and that was why a flyer at a chlorine-smelling community center could say free and mean it. She thought of her tuition statement. She thought of eleven pencil marks on a paper map. She caught herself wanting to believe that everything worked this way, and made herself stop, because wanting it did not make it true, and she was not in the business of mendacity even with herself, especially with herself.

She asked Priya about it the following Thursday, carefully, wanting confirmation rather than a lecture, and Priya just grinned and pulled up a page on the projector, an actual restored copy, plain white, plain black text, links underlined in blue. The class leaned forward. Even the teenagers who usually slumped sat up, and for a moment the room was enthralled by a page so plain it looked like a receipt, because it was the first one, the ancestor of everything they had ever scrolled. "It's still up," Priya said. "You can go look at it any time you want." Isabelle copied the address into her notebook, though she knew she would not need to.

The showcase came, and her site was small and crooked and it worked. Rose stood beside the borrowed projector in her church clothes and watched one of her Wednesday clients, Mr. Adeyemi, walk to the front and click his own name and check his own box, and the route updated, and the room applauded, and Rose gripped Isabelle's arm hard enough to hurt. There was still the loop Isabelle could not fix, still the tuition statement folded in her backpack, still everything she had not solved. But Mr. Adeyemi turned around with the mouse still in his hand and said, "Do it again," and she reached past him and clicked refresh.

Thomas skidded into the band practice room two minutes late, his trumpet case banging against his hip, and immediately wished he had stopped at the restroom first. The room smelled like old carpet and valve oil, and Marcus, who sat beside him every Tuesday, leaned away with a polite cough. "You okay over there, buddy?" Marcus asked, grinning but not mean about it. Thomas sniffed his own shirt and winced. He had run the whole way from gym class, and the practice room was small and warm, with the windows painted shut.

"Forgot my deodorant," Thomas admitted. "Left it in my locker."

Ms. Reyes kept a basket of supplies on the shelf by the tympani, and she waved him toward it without stopping her conversation with the flute section. Inside the basket Thomas found travel-size deodorant, little packets of wipes, and a sticky note in Ms. Reyes's round handwriting: "Wipe first, then deodorant. It works better on clean skin. Trust me." He ducked into the hallway, cleaned up, and rolled on the deodorant slowly and evenly, the way the note seemed to imply, instead of the quick two swipes he usually did at home. When he came back, Marcus raised his eyebrows in approval. "Much better. Now we can cooperate on this duet without me passing out."

They got through eight bars of the duet before Thomas's hiccups started. The first one hit in the middle of a held note and made his trumpet blurt like a sick goose. The second one came right after, and then a third. Marcus laughed so hard he dropped his mute. Thomas set the horn down and pressed his hand flat against his stomach, just below his lungs, where he could feel something jump every time a hiccup struck. He remembered a poster from health class, one he'd only half read: breathing was mostly done by a muscle down there, and a hiccup was that muscle suddenly spasming, with the vocal cords snapping shut right after.

So if the muscle was the problem, maybe slow breathing could get it to settle. He inhaled through his nose for a long count, held it, and let the air creep out even slower, keeping his hand pressed where the jumping had been. Marcus counted quietly along with him, tapping his foot. After the fourth slow breath, the next hiccup never arrived. Thomas waited, breathing the same careful way, and the room stayed quiet except for the radiator ticking.

"Did you just cure yourself?" Marcus asked.

Thomas picked up his trumpet, licked his lips, and lifted the mouthpiece toward the first note of the duet. "Count us in."

Declan had one hour before his bus came, and the library's research schedule said the science section was open until five. He marched past the front desk with brisk steps and dropped his backpack at a table near the window. His problem: he needed a topic for Monday's report, and so far his list had one word on it, "trees," which his teacher had called "a little too big."

He pulled a tall stack of books and started sorting them, comparing two things at once, how heavy each book was and how thick. The thickest ones were the heaviest, except for a giant atlas that was wide and heavy but thin. Funny, he thought, how two features can team up or argue.

Then a pinecone fell out of one book. It was small, sharp, and glued shut, like it was sealed with something sticky. "Did you chew gum and stick it on a pinecone?" he whispered to the empty book. The cone would not open, not even when he pressed it. So he hunted through the pages for an answer, flipping past diagrams and labels.

There it was. Some pine trees, like the lodgepole pine, have cones sealed with resin that only open in the heat of a wildfire, so the seeds drop onto freshly cleared ground. Declan read it twice. A fire could collapse the whole forest, and the tree's response was seeds? A burned forest could surprise hikers with thousands of new seedlings. It was almost like a trick.

He copied the fact onto his paper and grinned. "Fire helps the pine," he muttered. "Wait until my teacher hears that the tree was planning ahead." He put the little cone in his pocket, evidence for show and tell.

Addison stood in her grandmother's sunlit studio, surrounded by half-finished canvases and jars of brushes, holding a sculpture assignment that made her stomach tighten. The project was simple on the surface: create a three-dimensional animal form at twice the scale of a reference image. But when she'd sketched out her design for an ant, the proportions had looked wrong—impossibly fragile, like it would collapse under its own weight.

Her grandmother came in carrying a cup of tea, the steam curling between them. Grandma Rosa had been a painter before arthritis had reshaped her hands, and now she spent her afternoons in this room, teaching herself digital art with the same patient ferocity she'd once applied to oils. Addison showed her the sketches, explaining the voracious detail work ahead and her concern that the legs looked too thin for the body she'd planned.

"What if you made it smaller instead?" Grandma suggested, settling into the old leather chair with visible effort. "Not half the size. Different proportions entirely."

"That's not what the assignment asks for," Addison said, but she was already thinking. She pulled out her calculator and started writing down numbers. If she doubled the ant's length, what happened to its legs? She calculated the surface area of the original reference ant's leg, then doubled it. She multiplied by four. The doubled ant's leg would have four times as much surface area, which meant more material, more weight. She paused, her pencil hovering. But the leg itself got longer. And thicker, supposedly.

She did another calculation. If she actually doubled every dimension, the volume would multiply by eight. The ant's weight would go up by eight times. But the legs would only be four times stronger in cross-section. She wrote 8 ÷ 4 on her paper and stared at it. Two. The doubled ant would be twice as heavy relative to its leg strength.

"What are you working out over there?" Grandma asked, setting down her tea.

"I think I made a wrong assumption," Addison said slowly. "I thought if I just scaled everything up, it would work. Like, make the ant bigger, make the legs bigger, everything bigger." She looked up. "But that doesn't actually work."

She spent the next hour testing the relationship with different creatures, using objects in the studio as models. A small wooden bird Grandma had carved decades ago, a ceramic fish, an old plaster cast of an elephant leg. Each time she calculated, the same pattern emerged. She couldn't just rescind her original plan and expect a simple doubling to hold together.

When she finally returned to her ant design, she had completely reimagined it. The legs were thicker now, not proportionally longer but stockier, anchoring the body in a way that made physical sense. The exoskeleton would need reinforcement she'd originally missed. She began the armature with thick wire, building slowly, testing the structure as she went.

Three weeks later, Addison sat in the studio again, adding final details to a sculpture that looked nothing like her first sketches but felt right in her hands. The ant stood nearly three feet tall, its legs sturdy and real-looking, its form almost believable. She'd learned something that had nothing to do with art technique and everything to do with how the world actually worked.

"That's remarkable," her grandmother said, studying it from different angles. "You didn't just follow instructions. You figured out why."

Addison stepped back, her hands spotted with clay dust, looking at the creature she'd made. She reached out and adjusted one leg slightly, testing the weight distribution one more time.

Theodore's stomach growled so loudly during the spelling test that Marcus, two desks away, snickered. Theodore ignored him and kept writing. The words were tricky ones: "arrange," "mysterious," "product." When he wrote 6 times 4 equals 24 on the math section, he remembered that 24 was called a product, the answer you get when two numbers multiply. After the test, Mrs. Patel said the class could read quietly until lunch.

That was when the real problem started. Theodore's stomach growled again, even louder. How could he be this hungry? He had eaten a whole bowl of cereal at breakfast, and all he had done since then was sit at a desk. It seemed mysterious. Did thinking actually use up food? He decided to test it. He picked up a library book about the human body and flipped through the pages, hunting for the brain section.

"Are you reading about your stomach?" whispered Priya from the next desk.

"No, the brain," Theodore whispered back. "My stomach is mad at my brain, I think."

Then he found it, in a box on the page about energy. The brain, the book said, uses about 20 percent of the body's energy, even though it weighs only about 2 percent of the body's weight. Theodore read it twice. His brain was small and light compared to the rest of him, like a walnut next to a watermelon, yet it burned up a fifth of all his fuel. That spelling test had been real work, the kind that happens inside your head where nobody can see it.

He arranged the facts in order like sorting cards. Big and heavy body, low fuel use. Small and light brain, huge fuel use. Small things could need more than big things, if the small thing was a brain. So the strange hunger wasn't an excuse after all. It was math he could almost taste.

At lunch, Theodore told Marcus, "My brain ate a fifth of my breakfast, so I'm having two sandwiches."

"Brains don't eat sandwiches," said Marcus.

"Mine eats energy," said Theodore, and took an enormous bite.

Madison stared at the error message on her screen, the same red text she had been chasing for twenty minutes. The bootcamp had started three weeks ago, and she was supposed to be past the stage of building simple calculator programs, but here she was, stuck on a problem that probably meant nothing to anyone except her instructor and the twelve other people sweating through the same curriculum in the converted warehouse space they called Studio 9.

"You're thinking too hard," said Xavier from the desk beside hers. He was ebullient about everything—code, coffee, the fact that the vending machine had finally stocked the good granola bars—and it was either annoying or contagious, depending on the day. "What does the error actually say?"

"Index out of bounds," Madison read aloud. "I'm trying to loop through an array and pull out the temperature readings, but something's wrong with how I'm counting them."

Xavier rolled his chair over and leaned in. On his screen was a simple program that worked, clean lines of Python that did exactly what it was supposed to do. Madison had written nearly the same thing, but hers was breaking. She pointed to her loop. "I start at zero, go to ten."

"How many items are in your array?"

She scrolled up. Ten. She had ten readings. So zero through nine. Her face warmed. "Oh."

"Off by one," Xavier said, not unkindly. He rolled back to his own desk.

Madison fixed it, and the program ran. The calculator was absurd—it performed functions no one needed—but for the first time, she understood why the thing was breaking. The problem wasn't the concept. The problem was precision. Code did exactly what you told it to do, which meant if you were sloppy about what you wanted, it would be sloppy back at you.

That night, Madison found herself researching the history of the web instead of sleeping. She had seen something in the bootcamp materials about Tim Berners-Lee, but it was just a name attached to an image of a bearded man from the nineties. She wanted to know what he had actually built. The first web page went online in 1991 at CERN, she read, and Berners-Lee had invented the underlying technology. She kept scrolling.

In 1993, he had persuaded the lab to release the technology royalty-free.

Madison reread the sentence. The underlying technology. Everything. Released for free. She tried to imagine what that meant in reverse, tried to picture a world where the web belonged to CERN, where someone paid a fee to use HTML or make a website. The internet would be different. It might not exist the way it did. She thought about all the free websites she used, the ones that had shaped what she could access and learn and know, all of it built on infrastructure that could have been locked behind a paywall.

In bootcamp the next morning, she brought it up during the break. They were standing around the kitchen table where someone's mom had dropped off homemade brownies, and Madison mentioned what she had read.

"So basically he gave away his company," said Keisha, who was eating a brownie and thinking about something. "That's wild."

"He could have kept it," Madison said. "He could have made an annuity off it. Royalties forever."

"Would the web even exist like this if he hadn't?" Keisha asked.

"No," Xavier said. He was looking at the brownies. "It would be owned by one company. It would be expensive and restricted."

Madison thought about the calculator program, about how the bootcamp had cost her thirty-five hundred dollars, and how in three months she would have skills that people paid six figures for. She thought about how those skills existed because someone had decided not to aggrandize his control over them, had instead let them loose into the world. She had stumbled into this timeline where code was learnable, where bootcamps existed, where an eighteen-year-old without a degree could sit in a warehouse and actually become employable.

"But he didn't keep it," she said quietly.

Keisha bit into another brownie. "Makes you think about what you do with stuff you build, I guess. Whether you're building to own it or build to let it go."

Madison went back to her desk and opened her laptop. Her assignment was to write a program that converted currency, another small useless thing, but it would work. She put her fingers on the keyboard and began to think about what she wanted it to do.

Luca sat in the science circle with four other kids, waiting for Ms. Chen to start the discussion. Outside the classroom windows, snow dusted the playground, and Luca could see his breath when he pressed his nose close to the cold glass.

"Why do you think we have winter?" Ms. Chen asked the group.

"Because Earth moves far away from the sun," said Marcus right away. He sounded sure of himself. "We're like, way farther away in December, so it gets cold."

Luca nodded along with the others. That made sense. Things that move away from heat get colder, right? He thought about standing near a campfire and walking backward.

But then Ms. Chen asked them to look something up on the tablets. When Luca found the data about Earth's distance from the sun throughout the year, his eyes went wide. In early January, Earth was actually closest to the sun. Closest. Not farthest.

"Wait," Luca said. He reread the numbers to make sure. "If we're closer in January, why is it still super cold?"

The group got quiet. Marcus looked away from his tablet. Nobody had an answer.

Ms. Chen smiled. "That's the real question, isn't it? What do you think causes winter if it's not distance?"

Luca's mind spun. He thought about how the sun looked different in winter than summer. In summer, it climbed high in the sky and felt intense on his skin. In winter, it barely made it above the buildings, and its light seemed thin and pale. He paused and said, "Maybe it's not how close we are. Maybe it's like... the angle?"

"Explain what you mean," Ms. Chen said.

"If the sun is low in the sky, its heat gets spread out more when it hits the ground. Like if I shine a flashlight straight down it makes a bright spot, but if I tilt it sideways the light spreads out and gets weaker." He paused, then added, "The tilt of Earth must be different in winter."

Marcus leaned over and looked at Luca's tablet. His mouth opened. "You're right. It says here the tilt of Earth's axis is what causes seasons, not distance." He looked almost vulnerable as he admitted his mistake. "I was totally wrong."

Luca felt strange. Not like he'd won something, but like he'd watched Marcus describe the world one way, and then discovered it was actually different. He wondered how many other things people explained wrong, and how you figured out the real answers if you just listened to what everyone said.

"Good thinking, both of you," Ms. Chen said. "How would you paraphrase what you just discovered?"

Today was baking day at school. Aubrey got to make cookie dough. The dough was cold from the fridge. "Brrr, it is cold," she said. Miss Kim smiled. "Cold dough is easy to roll," she said.

Aubrey made round cookies. Then she made square cookies too. She put a letter on top of each one. One cookie had the letter A. Another had the letter B.

After baking, the class played a game. They rolled cookies down a small ramp. The round cookie went fast. It zipped all the way to the end! The square cookie did not zip. It bumped along. Then it stopped.

Aubrey tried again. The round cookie zipped. The square cookie bumped and stopped. She clapped her hands. "The round one has no corners," she said. "So it rolls smooth! The square one has corners. It bumps!"

Miss Kim gave her a hug. "Good thinking, Aubrey." Aubrey held up her round cookie with the letter A. "Round wheels are best," she said. Then she took a big, happy bite.

Victor stood at the soccer field with his coach. Today was his first real game. His stomach felt a little ill from being so nervous. Coach blew the whistle and Victor ran onto the grass.

The sun was very bright. Victor could not see the ball clearly. It flew past him and he missed it. He felt upset. At halftime, Coach pulled him to the side. "Watch your eyes when you come inside," Coach said. Victor did not understand what he meant.

That evening, Victor went into the dark bathroom at home. He held a flashlight and looked in the mirror. First, he shined the light away from his face. His eyes looked big and dark in the mirror. Next, he slowly moved the light toward his eyes. Then the dark spots in the middle of his eyes got smaller and smaller. He looked like a different person. Last, he moved the light away again and the dark spots grew big once more. Victor watched it happen again and again. The spots were holes that changed size.

The next game came on a cloudy day. Victor remembered what he had seen. He gave his eyes time to get used to the light before he played. He did not rush. His eyes felt ready. The ball came toward him and he saw it clearly. He ran fast and kicked it toward the goal.

Mohamed stood in the backyard with his baseball bat resting on his shoulder, watching his older cousin Jamal set up the net for practice. Today was going to be different. Today Mohamed wanted to figure out which sport he was actually better at: baseball or badminton.

His friend Keisha sat on the grass with a notebook. She had offered to keep score, and Mohamed appreciated that. He started with baseball first, hitting ten pitches that Jamal threw to him. He connected with seven of them, sending the ball sailing past the net. Then he switched to badminton. The birdie was so much lighter than a baseball. He swung harder, expecting to hit it far, but the birdie barely made it over the net. He hit five good shots out of ten tries. Baseball seemed like the obvious winner.

But something bothered Mohamed. When he swung the baseball bat fast, the impact made his ears ring a little. When he played badminton with a gentle swing, his ears felt fine. He mentioned this to Keisha. "That's weird," she said. "Why would hitting something hard affect your ears?"

Mohamed thought about this as he held both objects. The baseball was heavier and smaller. The badminton racket made a softer sound. Then it hit him. The baseball bat made a bigger, louder sound when it connected. Maybe loud sounds were doing something to his ears. He remembered something his mom had said once about how sound travels into your ear and makes things inside move. But how did that work exactly?

He held his hand against his ear and snapped his fingers quietly. Then he did it louder. With the loud snap, he felt his ear respond, like something inside was vibrating. He tried the same thing with Keisha snapping her fingers near his ear. The louder the snap, the more he could feel the movement.

"I think loud sounds make your insides move," Mohamed said slowly. "Like when you hit something really hard and it creates this big noise, your ear does more than just hear it."

Keisha's eyes widened. "So baseball makes bigger sounds, which means your ears have to work harder?"

Mohamed nodded and picked up the baseball bat again, feeling newly curious about the tiny bones inside his ears that had to vibrate every time he swung.
